1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Problem Definition}
5	\label{sec:method:problem}
6	
7	Let $f_\theta$ denote a language model and $\mathcal{D}_0$ a corpus of human-written seed text.
8	We define a \emph{recursive generation chain} of depth $K$ as the sequence $\mathcal{D}_0, \mathcal{D}_1, \dots, \mathcal{D}_K$, where each $\mathcal{D}_k$ ($k \geq 1$) is produced by finetuning $f_\theta$ on $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$ and sampling from the resulting model.
9	Depth $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text; depth $d{=}k$ ($k \geq 1$) denotes text generated by a model trained on depth-$(k{-}1)$ data.
10	
11	Given a text passage $x$, the task is to estimate its recursive generation depth $d \in \{0, 1, \dots, K\}$.
12	This is an ordinal classification problem: depths carry a natural ordering, and $d{=}1$ is structurally closer to $d{=}0$ than $d{=}3$ is, since each generation step compounds distributional drift.
13	
14	\subsection{Multi-Generational Benchmark Construction}
15	\label{sec:method:benchmark}
16	
17	We construct a benchmark spanning three axes: model family, decoding strategy, and generation depth.
18	
19	\paragraph{Model families.}
20	We select three 1--1.5B-parameter models with diverse pretraining corpora and architectures: Pythia-1.4B (EleutherAI), OLMo-1B (AI2), and GPT-2~XL (OpenAI, 1.5B).
21	Restricting to a narrow parameter range isolates the effect of architecture and training data from scale.
22	
23	\paragraph{Decoding strategies.}
24	Each model is paired with three decoding strategies: nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$) \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus}, temperature sampling ($\tau{=}0.9$), and top-$k$ sampling ($k{=}50$).
25	These span the dominant modes of open-ended generation and induce qualitatively different entropy profiles.
26	Our findings on feature importance and discriminability are limited to this grid; transfer to untested models, scales, or strategies is not established.
27	
28	\paragraph{Depth and scale.}
29	The primary benchmark covers depths d0--d3 across all $3 \times 3 = 9$ model--strategy cells, with 5{,}000 samples per depth per cell (180K samples total).
30	For depth extension experiments (\S\ref{sec:atlas}), we extend one pipeline (Pythia-1.4B, nucleus) to d0--d5.
31	
32	\paragraph{Generation pipeline.}
33	Starting from a Wikipedia subset as seed text ($\mathcal{D}_0$), each generation cycle proceeds in three steps: (1)~LoRA finetuning \cite{hu2022lora} with $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, lr $2{\times}10^{-4}$, batch size 8, 3 epochs, dropout $0.05$ (architecture-specific targets); (2)~unconditional generation of 5{,}000 passages (max 512 tokens, starting from BOS) under the specified decoding strategy; (3)~the generated corpus becomes $\mathcal{D}_k$ for the next cycle.
34	There is no per-passage lineage across depths, ensuring cross-validation splits do not introduce information leakage.
35	
36	\paragraph{Reference model.}
37	All statistical features (\S\ref{sec:method:features}) are computed using a fixed reference model---GPT-2 base (124M)---that is independent of the three generation models.
38	The reference model computes per-token perplexity for each passage, providing a consistent measurement frame across model families.
39	In cross-model leave-one-out evaluation (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), the reference model remains fixed even when GPT-2~XL is held out; the partial architectural overlap this introduces is discussed in Limitations.
40	
41	\subsection{Statistical Feature Design}
42	\label{sec:method:features}
43	
44	We extract a 19-dimensional feature vector $\mathbf{f}(x)$ from the reference-model perplexity distribution over each passage $x$.
45	The features fall into four categories (Table~\ref{tab:features}).
46	
47	\begin{table}[t]
48	\centering
49	\small
50	\caption{The 19 statistical features comprising $\mathbf{f}(x)$, grouped by category. All perplexity and surprisal features are computed from the reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).}
51	\label{tab:features}
52	\begin{tabular}{@{}llr@{}}
53	\toprule
54	Category & Features & $n$ \\
55	\midrule
56	Perplexity & mean, var, skewness, kurtosis, & 9 \\
57	statistics & p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 & \\
58	\addlinespace
59	Surprisal & mean, var, entropy & 3 \\
60	statistics & & \\
61	\addlinespace
62	Lexical & type--token ratio, hapax ratio, & 4 \\
63	diversity & bigram entropy, trigram entropy & \\
64	\addlinespace
65	Repetition & repeated 2/3/4-gram fractions & 3 \\
66	\bottomrule
67	\end{tabular}
68	\end{table}
69	
70	\emph{Perplexity statistics} (9 features) capture the per-token perplexity distribution via moments (mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis) and quantiles (p10--p90); tail quantiles prove especially informative as recursive finetuning erodes the high-perplexity tail (\S\ref{sec:atlas}).
71	\emph{Surprisal statistics} (3 features): mean, variance, and entropy of $-\log p(\text{token})$; surprisal variance captures second-order structure not redundant with perplexity moments.
72	\emph{Lexical diversity} (4 features): type--token ratio, hapax ratio, bigram/trigram entropy.
73	\emph{Repetition} (3 features): repeated $n$-gram fractions for $n \in \{2, 3, 4\}$.
74	
75	\subsection{Effective Discriminable Depth}
76	\label{sec:method:edd}
77	
78	Aggregate accuracy obscures whether discriminability degrades at specific depths.
79	We introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD): for each adjacent pair $(d, d{+}1)$, we train a dedicated binary RF (500 trees, 5-fold stratified CV) and compute AUC.
80	Given threshold $T$:
81	\begin{equation}
82	\mathrm{EDD}_T = \max \bigl\{ d^*{+}1 : \forall\, d' \leq d^*,\; \mathrm{AUC}(d', d'{+}1) \geq T \bigr\}
83	\label{eq:edd}
84	\end{equation}
85	where $d^* \in \{0, \dots, K{-}1\}$; $\mathrm{EDD}_T = 0$ if $\mathrm{AUC}(0,1) < T$.\footnote{Our AUC profiles are monotonically decreasing; for non-monotonic profiles, EDD reports the longest contiguous discriminable prefix (see Limitations).}
86	Default $T{=}0.75$; sensitivity at $T \in \{0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80\}$ in \S\ref{sec:atlas}.
87	Each AUC is from an independent binary classifier, avoiding decision boundary dilution (\S\ref{sec:atlas}).
88	
89	\paragraph{Classifiers.}
90	Our primary classifier is a Random Forest (200 trees, unconstrained depth, 5-fold stratified cross-validation).
91	We compare against CORAL ordinal regression \cite{coral2020}, DivEye \cite{diveye2026}, a 2-layer cross-entropy MLP, logistic regression, and a single-feature baseline using mean perplexity alone; results appear in \S\ref{sec:generalization}.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:intro}
3	
4	The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
5	As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone.

Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are consistent across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p90\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\textsc{var\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by importance in 9/9 and 8/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.

We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as an ordinal classification task and introduce a lightweight pipeline to solve it.
Given a text passage, we compute a 19-dimensional feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics---capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity---and classify it with a Random Forest into one of $K{+}1$ depth classes ($d{=}0$ for human text through $d{=}K$ for $K$-th generation text).
To systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and decoding strategies (nucleus $p{=}0.95$, temperature $\tau{=}0.9$, top-$k$ $k{=}50$), each spanning 4 generation depths, totaling 180K samples.
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories---temperature sampling accelerates convergence toward a low-entropy attractor, while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---and we introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Our contributions are:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Task formalization.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and introduce the EDD metric, which summarizes the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain separable above a given AUC threshold.

    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} We construct a systematic $3 \times 3$ map across model families and decoding strategies, revealing that \textsc{p90\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in all 9 cells and \textsc{var\_surprisal} in 8/9, with a mean Spearman rank correlation of $\rho{=}0.868$ across importance vectors. The extended Pythia nucleus pipeline (d0--d5) yields $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$, establishing that depth discrimination persists through four recursive steps before falling below threshold.

    \item \textbf{Generalization analysis.} Cross-model leave-one-out transfer achieves 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\% (chance = 25\%). We decompose a temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion into a scale component---partially correctable by per-strategy normalization---and a residual structural component that simple normalization cannot resolve.

    \item \textbf{End-to-end learning.} Both DeBERTa-v3-base (58.3\%) and RoBERTa-base (59.5\%) achieve ${\sim}$59\% via end-to-end finetuning---19pp below feature-based classifiers (78.2\%)---with the architecture-invariant gap ruling out model selection bias. Linear probing confirms that PLM representations cannot recover perplexity tail features (negative $R^2$), while SHAP analysis shows these features account for 88.8\% of RF's contribution.
\end{itemize}

1	\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	We formalized recursive generation depth estimation and showed that 19 statistical features achieve 70--85\% four-class accuracy ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$), with five features sufficing for 97.6\% of full performance and classifier-agnostic convergence within $\leq$0.4pp.
5	The dominant pair (\texttt{p90\_ppl} top-2 in 9/9 cells, \texttt{var\_surprisal} in 7/9) generalizes across model families without retraining, making depth estimation a measurable early warning for model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024_nature}---though cross-strategy transfer remains the bottleneck (59.1\% vs.\ 66.4\%) and all experiments use 1--1.5B models.
6	Future work should validate on mixed-domain corpora at larger scales and evaluate whether depth-graduated curation improves downstream training outcomes.
7

1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment constraint.}
5	Cross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling.
6	Per-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inversion (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC $0.24{\to}0.56$, OLMo $0.19{\to}0.70$) but leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (${\sim}0.83$), indicating that a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + strategy-conditioned classification) is needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.
7	
8	\paragraph{d0 inflation of headline metrics.}
9	Depth~0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall $>$98\% across all settings), inflating headline accuracy.
10	Cross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4\% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8\% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).
11	
12	\paragraph{Controlled vs.\ ecological setting.}
13	All experiments use Wikipedia seed text with controlled recursive generation (LoRA fine-tuning, 1--1.5B parameter models).
14	Depth signal is the dominant classification factor (5-fold CV 59--82\%, up to 2.5$\times$ chance): LOGO accuracy (72.1\%) matches standard CV (72.0\%), and seed-group prediction is at chance (10.2\% vs.\ 10\%; Appendix~\ref{app:domain_bias}).
15	Transfer to mixed-domain corpora, instruction-tuned models, and larger scales (7B+) remains open.
16	Real-world documents may also interleave segments at different recursion depths; extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity--statistical-power tradeoff.
17	
18	\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
19	Adversarial paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.
20	
21	\paragraph{EDD monotonicity assumption.}
22	Our EDD definition (Eq.~\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically---as observed in all our configurations.
23	However, \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).
24	Our cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.
25	In such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.
26	The choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.
27	
28	\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}
29	Surprisal-based features are computed relative to GPT-2 base (124M), introducing partial overlap when GPT-2~XL is held out, though GPT-2~XL holdout accuracy (67.6\%) does not exceed the unrelated OLMo (69.2\%).
30	The choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.
31	
32	\paragraph{Additional caveats.}
33	Detection features degrade under domain shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}; our depth features are likely susceptible.
34	\citet{falahati2026_curated} show that curated synthetic data need not trigger collapse, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.
35	
36	\section*{Ethics Statement}
37	
38	This work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.
39	No human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.
40	Our method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.

\begin{abstract}
As large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises---yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths.
From each passage we extract 19 statistical features---perplexity percentiles, surprisal moments, and lexical diversity measures---computed against a fixed reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).
A Random Forest classifier achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy (chance = 25\%; 58.8--82.6\% when excluding the near-perfectly separable d0 class; a zero-shot LLM baseline reaches only 36.2\%), with 90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance emerging as consistent depth markers across the studied $3 \times 3$ grid (top-2 importance in 9/9 and 7/9 cells, respectively).
Our \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas} reveals that decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories rather than merely attenuating them, and we define the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, finding $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ for extended recursion chains.
Cross-model transfer reaches 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\%; temperature sampling induces a d1/d2 AUC inversion that we decompose into a correctable scale component and a residual structural component.
Applied to 546 WikiText-103 passages, the classifier produces zero false positives despite $+$621\% domain shift in mean perplexity.
\end{abstract}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
\citet{shumailov2024_nature} demonstrate that recursive training on model outputs erodes distributional tails, collapsing the output distribution.
\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} formalize this via scaling laws distinguishing tail \emph{narrowing} from \emph{cutting}; \citet{dohmatob2024_strong_collapse} establish strong collapse guarantees, and \citet{dohmatob2024_demystified} analyze the regression case.
The MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} extends this to self-consuming models and quantifies the precision--recall tradeoff.
Mitigation strategies include retaining real data \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate} and filtering via detection \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse}.
Recent work identifies non-monotonic dynamics \cite{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement}, fixed-point convergence \cite{marchi2024_heat_death}, contamination bounds \cite{wang2026_contamination}, curated pipelines \cite{falahati2026_curated}, knowledge collapse \cite{knowledge_collapse2025}, spectral signatures \cite{sigma2026_spectral}, and self-improving loops \cite{synthetic_eggs2026}.
These works characterize degradation but assume depth is known a priori; we address the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt} introduced probability curvature as a zero-shot detection signal; Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024} improves efficiency via surrogate-model conditional curvature.
Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024} exploits perplexity ratios between related models, DivEye \cite{diveye2026} leverages surprisal diversity, and GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr} visualizes per-token likelihood ranks.
Fundamental limits exist: paraphrasing reduces detection to near chance \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase}, detection degrades under distribution shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and a generator barrier bounds performance when the generator is unknown \cite{pu2026_generator_barrier}.
Ghostbuster \cite{verma2024_ghostbuster} trains classifiers on statistical features for binary detection, sharing our feature-engineering philosophy but not addressing depth; M4-SemEval \cite{wang2024_m4_semeval} benchmarks multilingual detection, and DNA-GPT \cite{yang2024_dnagpt} uses divergent $n$-gram analysis.
Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} embeds detectable signals but requires proactive deployment.
All these methods perform binary classification, discarding ordinal depth information; our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.

\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates editing extent but does not model recursive chains.
\citet{uchendu2020_attribution} classify \emph{which} model generated text rather than recursion depth.
LOKI \cite{loki2025} benchmarks synthetic data detection across modalities but evaluates binary detection only.
\citet{mohamed2025_broken_telephone} study iterative generation as a ``broken telephone'' effect, measuring forward degradation; our task performs the inverse, classifying depth from text alone.

\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
CORAL \cite{coral2020} enforces rank consistency via ordered binary tasks; CLOC \cite{cloc2025} extends contrastive learning with multi-margin ordinal losses.
We adopt both as baselines (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) to confirm the signal is accessible to principled ordinal methods.

\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
Decoding strategies shape text statistics in ways that interact with depth signals: nucleus sampling maintains diversity \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus}, decoding parameters affect evaluation non-trivially \cite{finlayson2024_closing}, and strategy effects are model-dependent \cite{garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded}.
\citet{wiher2022_decoding} systematically compare methods on surface-level properties, and Mirostat \cite{basu2021_mirostat} regulates output entropy via perplexity control.
Our Depth Degradation Atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) reveals that these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation---temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---effects beyond single-pass text quality.

Source attribution \cite{uchendu2020_attribution} identifies the generating model but not the generation history.
Depth estimation characterizes \emph{iterative reuse} regardless of generator cooperation or identity.
-A layered provenance system combining these three signals---watermark presence, source model, and recursion depth---could support more nuanced data auditing than any single method.
